en.name: *The Prodigal Son*
description:
The painting only became part of the Borghese collection in the 19th century, having earlier been mentioned in the collection of Prince Lancellotti, although the details of its commissioning are unknown. The canvas (1627–1628) reworks an earlier piece completed 10 years before for Cardinal Serra in Ferrara.  
The subject is taken from the parable of the prodigal son from the Gospel of St. Luke (15, 11–32). It tells of the forgiveness of a father who welcomes his youngest son after he has squandered his inheritance and been reduced to poverty and hunger. The scene in the canvas focuses on the moment when the aged father, shown in the centre of the composition, having found his son in such miserable conditions – rendered with marked realism in the rags tied around his waist – orders his servant to give him decent clothing. The boy is in fact busy putting on a clean shirt. The idea of a return to domestic intimacy is suggested by the closed window, in which the painter accurately renders the reflection of light.  
Guercino was able to portray this moment of family intimacy with great tenderness, in particular the detail of the dog resting his paws on the young man's lap, pleased that his master has returned home. The presence of the dog also enhances the symbolic idea of faithfulness often attributed to them, in accordance with allegorical custom in the Baroque tradition. This virtue is related to mercy according to the meaning given in the parable: the teaching that Christ imparted to his followers.  
Guercino, renowned as a painter of emotions, clearly shows here the father's forgiveness; he believed that his son was dead before he found him. From a stylistic point of view, we can see the influence of Venetian colourism, which Guercino had acquired on his trip to Venice in 1618, and which the artists blends together in a measured composition of classical inspiration.

In this painting, the colours are clearly influenced by Venetian art (Guercino stayed in Venice in 1618) combined with the more classical design of the figure.  
Guercino, renowned as a painter of “emotions” here clearly represents the forgiveness of a father who believing his son to be dead, is re-united with him.
artist: Giovan Francesco Barbieri, also known as Il Guercino
keywords: Venetian influence; realism; Christian themes; animal decoration; symbol; zoomorphic imagery; allegory; classical model

it.name: *Ritorno del figliol prodigo*
description: Il dipinto è entrato nelle collezioni Borghese solo nell'800; prima è ricordato nelle collezioni del principe Lancellotti, anche se le vicende legate alla sua commissione non sono note. La tela, del 1627-28, rielabora una precedente opera eseguita dieci anni prima per il cardinal Serra a Ferrara. Il soggetto è tratto dalla parabola del figliol prodigo, riportata nel Vangelo di Luca ( 15, 11-32). Qui si narra del perdono di un padre che accoglie il figlio minore dopo che questi ha sperperato la sua parte di eredità, rimanendo povero e affamato. La scena della tela fissa il momento in cui l'anziano genitore, raffigurato al centro della composizione, avendo trovato il figlio in condizioni tanto miserevoli – rese con estremo realismo dal cencio annodato alla vita – ordina al servo di porgergli vesti dignitose. Il ragazzo è infatti intento ad indossare la candida camicia.  L'idea del ritorno all'intimità domestica è suggerita dalla finestra chiusa, in cui il pittore rende accuratamente il riflesso della luce. Guercino ha saputo restituire con estrema tenerezza il particolare momento di intimità familiare, si noti il dettaglio del cane che poggia le zampe sul grembo del giovane, felice del ritorno a casa del padrone. La presenza dell'animale, inoltre, sottolinea, secondo le consuete allegorie della cultura barocca, la nota simbologia di fedeltà  che solitamente gli è riconosciuta. Virtù questa legata alla misericordia, secondo il significato dato alla parabola, cioè l'insegnamento che Cristo ha lasciato ai suoi fedeli. Guercino, noto come pittore degli “affetti”, ha qui ben evidenziato il perdono di un padre che credeva il figlio morto e che invece ha ritrovato. Dal punto di vista stilistico, vi si riconoscono gli influssi del colorismo veneto, acquisito direttamente da Guercino durante il soggiorno a Venezia nel 1618, che l'artista fonde nella calibrata composizione di ispirazione classicista.

In questo dipinto i colori mostrano una chiara influenza dell'arte veneziana (andò a Venezia nel 1618) combinati ad un disegno più classico delle figure.  
Guercino, noto come pittore degli “affetti”, ha qui ben evidenziato il perdono di un padre che credeva il figlio morto e che invece ha ritrovato.
artist: Giovan Francesco Barbieri, detto Il Guercino
keywords: Influenza veneziana; realismo; tematiche cristiane; decorazione con animali; immaginario zoomorfico; allegorie; modello classico

ar.name: مبخرة ، جذع أسد
description: جذع الأسد هذا يبدو أنه جزء من مبخرة. ولكن على عكس الأشكال الأخرى المعروفة فإن نمط  الوظيفة مختلف. وتتألف القطعة من جسم حيوان يشبه القط مع قائمتيه الأماميتان والنهايتين بشكل شوكة مخروطية نهايتها مكسورة. ويبدي جسم القطعة وجود حجرة مجوفة التي تقع تماما خلف صدر القط والذي بدوره يبدي عملا مخرما. والعمل المخرم مكون من درجة من سعيفات النخل بشكل قلب مقلوب. والنهايات ملفوفة على بعضها وأيضا تتألف من سعيفات نخل. وفوق العنق المطاول يقع الرأس ذو الوجه المتجه لأعلى. وهو يتميز بقص دقيق واضح مع أنف بارز. والعينين و الفم أيضا مثقبة.  وكل التفاصيل الأخرى مبينة عن طريق النحت. والأرجل هي طويلة ونحيلة ومحنية بشكل طفيف ويمكن أن تكون قد صبت بشكل منفصل.هناك العديد من الأنواع المعروفة لمباخر بشكل حيوان. وأكثرها شيوعا هو النوع الذي له رأس يمكن أن يطوى للخلف ليفتح الوعاء ويوضع البخور فيه. لكن هذا المثال يبدو أنه يعمل  مثل جارور. والبخور يمكن وضعه بسهولة في الحجرة المجوفة والقطعة توضع بعد ذلك في النصف الآخر من التشكيل حيث تضمن النهاية المخروطية عملها كقاعدة وأرجل لتحملها.
keywords: مبخرة ، أسد ، مشغولة معدنية
partner: المتحف الجامعي للفن الإسلامي / مجموعة بوميلر

en.name: Incense Burner, Lion Torso
description:
This lion torso seems to be part of an incense burner. But, in contrast to other known forms, the mode of function is different. The object consists of the torso of a cat-like animal with its two front legs and ends in a sharp, conical thorn, the end of which is broken off. The body of the object features a hollow chamber that lies right behind the chest of the cat, which in turn shows openwork. The openwork is made of a palmette tendril in the shape of an upside-down heart. The ends are intertwined and also consist of palmettes. Above the elongated neck sits the upwardly faced head. Its features are clear cut with a prominent nose. The eyes and mouth are also perforated. All other details are indicated through carvings. The legs are long and slender, slightly bent, and could have been cast separately.  
There are many known types of animal-shaped incense burners. The most common is a type where the head can be folded backwards to open the vessel and place the incense in. However, this example seems to work like a drawer. The incense could easily be placed into the hollow chamber and the object is then presumably pushed into the other half of the artifact, with the conical ending ensuring its foothold.
holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
keywords: Incense burner; lion; metalwork
partner: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection

en.name: Baking flatbread in a *tannur* in an Assyrian village in northeast Syria
description:
Inhabitants of the western mountain areas and parts of northeast Syria bake the thicker (1–2 cm) flatbread that is baked on the wall of a bulbous vertical clay oven (*tannur*). To achieve the required temperature of the oven wall the firewood must be burnt down to embers.  
These ovens consist of an interior part made from clay mixed with goat hair and chaff, which is fired to become the inner wall. If the *tannur* should be placed above the ground, it will be given a thick coating of at least 30 cm from pieces of sun-dried mud brick and mortar, with a worktop to the side. These huge ovens are often placed in the corner of the courtyard or sometimes outside the compound as a common oven. In Syria rarely is a *tannur* dug into the ground, like the one in the photo taken in an Assyrian village in the Upper Khabur valley.  
The *tannur* bread (*hubz tannur*) requires more time to prepare, as yeast is added, and the dough is kneaded intensively. Preferably local wheat is used.

en.name: Arab / Bedouin Gun
short_description: This matchlock musket, locally made based on a European prototype, is known as 'Abu Futtila'. It is an  example of the type of weapon used from the early 18th century until as late as the early 20th century in the Arabian Peninsula. The type was typically simply stocked, but generally as with this example, fitted with an extremely high quality barrel.  The tang is stamped with a maker's mark. This gun is a good example as it retains what is possibly its original match consisting of twisted fibre cord bound with cotton and two large copper alloy tubular fittings,  probably to hold lighted sections of the match. The gun is muzzle loaded and has a  .50 calibre smoothbore barrel with a single shot firing capacity. The musket shows fine fluting and has a chiseled barrel with geometric designs and silver inlay, as well as a copper alloy mounted forward grip. The copper taper holders under the wick do not appear to be original, but this gun still has its primer pan protector.Weapons were among the most coveted and desirable, if often illicit commodities in the Arab Gulf. European weapons were mainly imported through Muscat and Bushire on the Persian coast of the Gulf, with many than copied locally.
holder: Sharjah Al-Hisn Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
keywords: Abu Futtila

en.name: Léon Bollée Voiturette
description: Automaking was something of a Bollée family business: Léon's father and brother, both named Amédée, were renowned French pioneers of steam transmission. Starting in 1895 Léon built tricycles gave them the name of "voiturette", a name that later would become generic for small cars. This 3-wheeler was also popularly known as "la Tue Belle-mère" (mother-in-law murderer), because the passenger was seated up front. It has no suspension but is capable of reaching a potentially dangerous speed of 30km/h. The voiturette claimed first and second places in the first ever London-Brighton Run, in 1896. Notice the small steering wheel, an innovation at the time.
keywords: Early motorcar; chain drive; wood wheels; single-cylinder

de.name: Kanzel
description: Die mit ihrem leicht geschwungenem Korb und Schalldeckel in spätbarocker Tradition stehende Kanzel wurde 1784 in Zusammenarbeit dreier Künstler vollendet, dem Tischler Michael Hueber, dem Stukkator Graßmayr und dem Bildhauer Paterer, der den Schalldeckel mit den Figuren eines guten Hirten und vier Engeln bekrönte.
artist: Michael Hueber; Franz Graßmayr; Johann Paterer

en.name: Pulpit
description: The gently curved pulpit and baldachin in the Late Baroque tradition was completed in 1784 and is the work of three artists, the carpenter Michael Hueber, the stucco mason Graßmayr and the sculptor Paterer who crowned the baldachin with the figures of a good shepherd and four angels.
artist: Michael Hueber [n.d.]; Franz Graßmayr [n.d.]; Johann Paterer (1712–1785)

en.name: Mosque of Sultan al-Mu'ayyad Shaykh
description:
Sultan al-Mu’ayyad Shaykh had this mosque built on the site of the prison in which he had been confined while an *amir* under Sultan Farag Ibn Barquq. He vowed to turn the prison into a place of study and prayer should God ever bestow upon him the honour of ruling Egypt. In 818/1415 construction began. This vast pious foundation was to include a congregational mosque, three minarets, two mausoleums and a *madrasa* for the four rites for Sufi students. On al-Mu’ayyad Shaykh’s death, the building had not reached completion. It is one of Cairo’s largest mosques and when the Ottoman Sultan Salim I saw it, he is said to have exclaimed “It is indeed a building fit for kings”.  
It has been called the mosque of sin by some historians due to the fact that some of its furnishings were taken from other buildings. Despite having spent enormous sums of money on the construction and furnishing of the building, when al-Mu’ayyad could not afford costly materials he expropriated them from other earlier foundations. In spite of paying for their removal, such practice was deemed illegal given that once a complex had been furnished, both its buildings and its fittings could no longer change hands. All the same he paid 500 dinars for the lamps and main entrance-door panels faced in bronze and inlaid with metal originally from the Sultan Hassan complex (I.1.g). The marble panels and friezes come from the *qibla* wall in the Mosque of Qusun and from other mosques and houses. Sultan al-Mu’ayyad made his *amirs* pay for the paintings in the mosque and the artisans for the expenses on carpentry and wood decoration.  
decoration. The main entrance on the south east façade is decorated in alternating bands of black and white marble and crowned by a tri-lobed arch. Its deep recess is crowned with a vault of nine rows of *muqarnas*, all of which are enclosed in a rectangular frame rising above the cornice, characteristic of Iranian architectural origins. The door-jambs and the lintel of pink granite are framed in a white interlaced band with earthenware red and turquoise incrustations. The entrance leads to a *derka*, where a cross vault rises above it. To the right there is a passageway paved in marble leading to the mosque courtyard, in the centre of which an ablutions font replaces the old fountain. To the left we gain access to the mausoleum in which the Sultan and his oldest son Ibrahim are buried.  
The *mihrab* in the square mausoleum is decorated with marble and a dome resting on *muqarnas* pendentives rises above it. On the outside, the dome is decorated with the same horizontal zigzag design as the domes of the *khanqa* of Farag Ibn Barquq. The prayer hall was to be flanked on either side by a domed mausoleum, but only the tombs of the Sultan and his son are housed in such a way. The second mausoleum, set apart for the women and covered by a flat roof, is located to the south of the *qibla* hall, at the foot of one of the two minarets.  
Of the three minarets along the southwest axis of the building, the westernmost one collapsed. The other two, supported by the towers of Bab Zuwayla, also collapsed not long after being built in 842/1438; they were soon reconstructed.  
With the use of the towers of Bab Zuwayla as the base for the two minarets, they dominate the skyline from a distance clearly visible from the Citadel. The two minarets with their octagonal section shafts and transitions each separated by a balcony resting on a *muqarnas* cornice, and *gawsaq* crowned with a bulbiform top standing 50 m. high above street level, have become a symbol of the city of Cairo.  
The mosque layout follows the lines of the traditional hypostyle mosque plan. The central courtyard was originally surrounded by four porticoes. Today only one remains, that of the *qibla* wall. Archaeological excavations have revealed that the other three sides comprised a double aisle divided by an arcade. Parallel to the *qibla* wall, three rows of marble columns uphold the richly decorated wooden ceiling. The walls around the sanctuary are covered by coloured marble panels, which originated from earlier buildings. The richest decoration was naturally reserved for the *qibla* wall. The high panelling at the base of the *mihrab* is divided into two areas by differing types of marble decoration and crowned by a frieze of paired colonettes in turquoise blue. To its right is the original wooden *minbar*; it is decorated in mother-of-pearl and ivory inlay, a magnificent example of the richness of carpentry at the time. The marble *dikkat al-muballigh* (recitation platform), supported on eight marble columns, is located in the second aisle of the *qibla* hall.  
Its extensive provision of over 200 rooms for students and its large library brought recognition to the mosque as a renowned academic institution in the 9th/15th century. Its academic chairs were held by the most eminent of scholars such as Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani (b.774/1372 d.853/1449) from Ascalon, (an ancient city of Palestine), an expert in interpretation of the Qur’an.

es.name: Mezquita del Sultán al-Mu’ayyad Chayj
description:
El sultán al-Mu’ayyad Chayj construyó esta mezquita en el lugar que ocupaba la cárcel donde fue confinado cuando era emir del sultán Farag Ibn Barquq. Hizo voto de transformar la prisión en lugar de estudio y oración, si Dios le concedía ser soberano de Egipto. La vasta fundación piadosa, que incluía una mezquita *aljama*, tres alminares, dos mausoleos y una *madrasa* para los cuatro ritos destinada a estudiantes sufíes, fue comenzada en 818/1415; a la muerte del sultán aún no se había terminado. Es una de las mayores mezquitas de El Cairo, y cuando el sultán otomano Salim I la contempló, exclamó: “Ciertamente, este es un edificio de reyes”.  
Algunos historiadores se refieren a ella como la mezquita del pecado, debido a que el sultán al-Mu’ayyad tomó muchos de sus componentes de otros edificios. Aunque gastó cuantiosas sumas en la construcción y dotación del edificio, cuando no podía disponer de materiales costosos expropiaba elementos de fundaciones anteriores. Pese a que pagaba las dotaciones de estas, la práctica seguía siendo ilegal, pues una vez entregados, los edificios y sus accesiones ya no podían cambiar de propietario. Así es que pagó con 500 dinares las arañas y los batientes de la puerta principal del complejo del sultán Hasan (I.1.g), revestidos de bronce y damasquinados. Los grandes paneles, los rodapiés y los frisos de mármol proceden del muro de la *qibla* de la mezquita de Qusun, y de otras mezquitas y casas. El sultán impuso a sus emires la obligación de pagar las pinturas de la mezquita, y a los artesanos que se hiciesen cargo de los gastos de los trabajos en madera.  
En la fachada sureste, la entrada, revestida en bandas alternadas de mármol blanco y negro y coronada por un arco trilobulado, se compone de un profundo nicho techado por una bóveda de 9 hileras de mocárabes; todo ello encajado en un marco rectangular que se eleva sobre la cornisa, característica muy difundida en la arquitectura iraní. Las jambas y el dintel de granito rosa están enmarcados por una banda blanca entrelazada, con incrustaciones de cerámica en rojo y turquesa. La entrada conduce a una *derka*, cubierta con una bóveda de crucería; desde la derecha, a través de un pasillo enlosado en mármol, se accede al patio de la mezquita, donde una pila para las abluciones rituales sustituye a la antigua fuente central; y por la izquierda se entra al mausoleo donde están enterrados el sultán y su hijo mayor Ibrahim. De superficie cuadrada, dispone de un *mihrab* decorado con mármol y está cubierto por una cúpula sobre pechinas de varias hileras de mocárabes, decorada en su parte exterior con bandas horizontales de zigzag, igual que las cúpulas de la *janqa* de Farag Ibn Barquq. De la misma manera, la sala de oración había de ir flanqueada por dos mausoleos con cúpula, pero solo la tiene el que contiene los cenotafios del sultán y su hijo. El segundo mausoleo, reservado a las mujeres y cubierto por un techo plano, está situado en el extremo sur de la sala de la *qibla*, al pie de uno de los dos alminares.  
De los tres alminares dispuestos en el eje suroeste, el del extremo oeste se derrumbó. Los otros dos, apoyados en las torres de Bab Zuwayla, también se cayeron poco después de su construcción en el año 842/1438, pero fueron reconstruidos en breve tiempo.  
El empleo de las torres de Bab Zuwayla como base de los alminares dio a estos una preeminencia que los hace claramente visibles desde la Ciudadela, a gran distancia. Con sus dos fustes octogonales y el *gawsaq* coronado con un florón bulbiforme —cada transición marcada por un balcón sobre una cornisa de mocárabes— se elevan unos 50 m por encima del nivel de la calle y son el emblema de la Ciudad de El Cairo.  
La planta de la mezquita sigue el modelo de las mezquitas hipóstilas tradicionales; el patio central descubierto estaba originariamente rodeado de cuatro pórticos, pero solo se ha conservado la sala de oración en el lado de la *qibla*. Las excavaciones arqueológicas realizadas han demostrado que los otros tres pórticos estaban formados por dos naves, separadas por una arquería.  
Tres hileras de columnas de mármol, paralelas al muro de la *qibla*, sostienen un techo de madera lujosamente decorado. Todas las paredes de la sala de la *qibla* están cubiertas de mármol policromo procedente de edificios anteriores, aunque la decoración más importante se reservó para el muro de la *qibla*. El alto zócalo del *mihrab*, dividido en dos zonas diferenciadas por el tipo de ornamentación con mármol, está coronado por un friso de columnitas geminadas de color azul turquesa. A su derecha se alza el originario *mimbar* de madera, realizado con pequeñas piezas ensambladas y taraceadas con nácar y marfil, magnífico ejemplo de la riqueza de la carpintería contemporánea. En el centro de la segunda nave de la sala de la *qibla*, la *dikkat al-muballig* (tribuna del repetidor) de mármol está sostenida por 8 columnas del mismo material.  
Su amplia dotación con más de 200 habitaciones para estudiantes y su gran biblioteca hicieron de esta mezquita una de las instituciones académicas más destacadas del siglo IX/XV; sus cátedras fueron ocupadas por los estudiosos más eminentes, como Ibn Hayar al-Asqalani (774/1372-853/1449), originario de Ascalón (antigua ciudad de Palestina) y experto en interpretación coránica.

fr.name: Mosquée du Sultan al-Mu’ayyad Cheikh
description:
Le sultan al-Mu’ayyad Cheikh construisit la mosquée sur l’emplacement qu’occupait la prison où il fut incarcéré lorsqu’il était émir du sultan Farag Ibn Barquq. Il fit le voeu de transformer la prison en lieu d’étude et de prière si Dieu lui accordait de devenir souverain d’Égypte. La vaste fondation pieuse, qui incluait une Grande Mosquée, trois minarets, deux mausolées et une *madrasa* pour les quatre rites destinée aux étudiants soufis, fut commencée en 818/1415; à la mort du sultan, elle n’était pas encore achevée. C’est l’une des plus grandes mosquées du Caire, et lorsque le sultan ottoman Sélim Ier la contempla, il s’exclama: “À l’évidence, cet édifice est un édifice de rois.” Quelques historiens l’évoquent comme la mosquée du péché, parce que le sultan al- Mu’ayyad préleva nombre de ses éléments sur d’autres mosquées. Bien qu’il ait investi des sommes colossales dans la construction et la dotation de l’édifice, lorsqu’il ne pouvait disposer de matériaux coûteux, il s’appropriait des éléments de fondations plus anciennes. Même s’il s’acquittait des dotations de ces dernières, la pratique n’en était pas moins inique, étant donné qu’une fois qu’ils étaient dotés, les édifices et leur mobilier ne pouvaient plus changer de propriétaire. C’est ainsi qu’il paya 500 dinars les lustres et les battants de la porte principale revêtus de bronze damasquiné du complexe du sultan Hassan (I.1.g). Les grands panneaux, les plinthes et les frises de marbre proviennent du mur qibla de la mosquée de Qusun, ainsi que d’autres mosquées et demeures. Le sultan obligea ses émirs à payer les peintures de la mosquée, et les artisans furent contraints de prendre à leur charge les dépenses des travaux en bois.  
Sur la façade sud-est, l’entrée, revêtue de bandeaux alternés de marbre blanc et noir et surmontée d’un arc trilobé, est composée d’une profonde niche couronnée d’une voûte de 9 rangées de *mouqarna*s; l’ensemble est inscrit dans un encadrement rectangulaire s’élevant au-dessus de la corniche, une caractéristique très répandue dans l’architecture iranienne. Les piédroits et le linteau de granit rose sont encadrés d’une bande blanche entrelacée à incrustations d’argile rouge et turquoise. L’entrée conduit à une *derka*, couverte d’une voûte d’ogives; sur la droite, un corridor à dallage de marbre conduit à la cour de la mosquée, dans laquelle un bassin à ablutions rituelles remplace l’ancienne fontaine centrale; et par la gauche on accède au mausolée où sont enterrés le sultan et son fils aîné Ibrahim. De forme carrée, il dispose d’un *mihrab* orné de marbre et est surmonté d’une coupole sur pendentifs à plusieurs rangées de *mouqarna*s, dont l’extérieur est décoré de bandes horizontales de zigzags identiques à ceux des coupoles de la *khanqa* de Farag Ibn Barquq. De la même façon, la salle de prière devait être flanquée de deux mausolées à coupole, mais seul le mausolée qui abrite les cénotaphes du sultan et de son fils en est encore surmonté. Le second mausolée, réservé aux femmes et couvert d’un plafond plat, se trouve à l’extrémité sud de la salle de la *qibla*, au pied de l’un des deux minarets.  
Des trois minarets orientés dans l’axe sud-ouest, celui de l’extrémité ouest s’est effondré. Les deux autres, qui s’appuient sur les tours de Bab Zuwayla, sont également tombés peu après leur construction en 842/1438, mais ils ont été reconstruits peu de temps après.  
Le fait que les tours de Bab Zuwayla aient été utilisées comme bases des minarets confère à ces derniers une prééminence qui les rend parfaitement visibles depuis la Citadelle, pourtant fort éloignée. Avec ses deux fûts octogonaux et le *gawsaq* couronné d’un fleuron bulbiforme – chaque transition étant soulignée par un balcon sur corniche de *mouqarna*s –, ils s’élèvent à quelque 50 m au-dessus du niveau de la rue et sont l’emblème de la ville du Caire. Le plan de la mosquée obéit au modèle des mosquées hypostyles traditionnelles; la cour centrale découverte était à l’origine entourée de quatre portiques, mais seule la salle de prière, sur le côté de la *qibla*, a survécu. Les fouilles archéologiques réalisées sur place ont montré que les trois autres portiques étaient composés de deux nefs séparées par des arcades.  
Parallèles au mur de la *qibla*, trois rangées de colonnes de marbre soutiennent un toit de bois luxueusement décoré. Tous les murs de la salle de la *qibla* sont plaqués de marbre de couleur provenant d’édifices plus anciens, mais c’est au mur de la *qibla* que fut réservée la plus grande emphase décorative. Le haut socle du *mihrab*, divisé en deux zones différenciées par le type d’ornementation de marbre, est couronné d’une frise de paires de colonnettes bleu turquoise. À sa droite s’élève le *minbar* d’origine, en bois, dont l’ornementation en assemblage de fines pièces de bois marquetées de marbre et de nacre en fait un magnifique témoignage de la richesse de l’ébénisterie de l’époque. Au centre de la seconde nef de la salle de la *qibla*, la *dikkat al-muballigh* (tribune du répétiteur) en marbre repose sur 8 colonnes également en marbre.  
Son ample dotation, avec plus de 200 chambres pour les étudiants et sa grande bibliothèque, fit de cette mosquée une des institutions éducatives les plus réputées du IXe/XVe siècle; ses chaires furent occupées par les plus éminents érudits, tels Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani (774/1372- 853/1449), originaire d’Ascalon (une ancienne ville de Palestine) et expert en interprétation coranique.

en.name: Table jar with blue glaze
description: This table jar, unearthed in 1981 during the French mission at the Murwab site in one of the houses with a plaster floor, exhibits a well-recognized design inspired by early Islamic metal needles. Featuring a notably tall (10cm) and wide (11cm rim diameter) straight neck with a slightly projecting rim, the jar boasts a mildly globular body that accommodates two handles on its upper portion. The straight handles suspend from the upper part of the neck. Although the blue glaze is considerably damaged, it reveals a very fine cream paste akin to eggshell. This artefact likely originated from the workshops of Basra.
dates: Hegira late 2nd to late 3rd century / AD late 8th to late 9th century
keywords: earthenware, storage, transportation, jar

en.name: Garden of the Bishop’s Palace
description:
Gardens held a central place in 17th- and 18th- century European art. The Baroque garden sought to represent the universe, symbolically blending aesthetic values with philosophical ideals. Sometimes large in scale, usually complex, and rich in terms of decoration, they combined nature with ornamental elements such as in Portuguese statues and *azulejos* (tile panels), reflecting the social status and the customs of their patrons. The ecclesiastical garden was an excellent vehicle for the diversion, spiritual exaltation and social projection of both the resident and his visitors.  
The Garden of the Bishop's Palace was probably conceived as a space for the celebration of God through the allegories and examples of virtue it expounded. In the intermediate rectangular terrace divided into three longitudinal axes with a central lake and four others at the corners, granite sculptures depict the spiritual world (representing the Four Cardinal and Three Theological Virtues as well as the Apostles in the monumental Apostles' Stairway), the material world (signs of the Zodiac, the Four Continents, Seasons and Four Elements) and lastly the national reality (a monumental Kings' Stairway with images of the Portuguese kings). The several different levels of the garden are connected by stairways.  
The Lake of the Crowns and a curious overflow garden named *Jardim Alagado* occupy the same level, from which two monumental stairways lead to the upper level where the Water Tank and the Moses Cascade, a purely a decorative feature, are situated.
The Garden of the Bishop’s palace combines lakes, fountains, flowerbeds and stone sculptures representing religious themes, pagan personalities and the kings of Portugal.
history: The Garden of the Bishops of Castelo Branco was conceived in the first quarter of the 18th century by the Bishop of Guarda, João de Mendonça (1711–1736), who built it close to the Winter Palace which he used to avoid the freezing temperatures of winter in Guarda. In 1771, the Diocese of Castelo Branco was created, and the former Winter Palace became the Bishop's official residence. The Garden was completed at the end of the 18th century under the direction of D. Vicente Ferrer da Rocha, second Bishop of Castelo Branco, assisted by Fr. Daniel Joaquim do Rosário. At the beginning of the 20th century, a new level at the entrance of the main terrace was installed. It is decorated with flower beds surrounded by hedges and *azulejos* depicting the Bishops of Castelo Branco.
keywords: Garden, allegory, cardinal and theological virtues, water architecture; Castelo Branco
tags: Garden, allegory, cardinal and theological virtues, water architecture
partner: Institute for the Administration of Architectural and Archaeological Heritage -  IGESPAR

pt.name: *Jardim do Paço Episcopal*
description:
Os jardins desempenharam um papel relevante no contexto da arte europeia dos séculos XVII e XVIII.  
Os jardins barrocos tentavam representar o Universo de uma forma simbólica, combinando valores estéticos com conceitos filosóficos. Por vezes de dimensão considerável e com uma composição rica e elaborada, combinavam a natureza com elementos ornamentais, tais como estátuas e painéis de azulejos, no caso português, reflectindo assim os hábitos sociais e culturais dos encomendadores. Em suma, funcionavam como palco de diversão, projecção social ou exaltação espiritual, no caso dos espaços clericais.  
O Jardim do Paço Episcopal, constituído por diferentes patamares ligados por escadarias, deve ser entendido como um espaço de evocação a Deus pela alegoria e pelo exemplo das virtudes. No patamar intermédio, de planta rectangular e dividido longitudinalmente em três partes, com um lago central e mais quatro aos cantos, estátuas em granito representam as Escrituras e o mundo espiritual, (quatro virtudes cardinais, três virtudes teologais e monumental Escadaria dos Apóstolos que liga ao patamar superior); o mundo material (signos, continentes, estações do ano e os quatro elementos) e, por fim, o mundo nacional, através da monumental Escadaria dos Reis (ao fundo, também ligando ao patamar superior).  
No mesmo patamar, está o Tanque das Coroas, bem como um jardim particularmente curioso, conhecido por *Jardim Alagado.*  
No patamar superior, encontra-se um tanque grande, decorado com a Cascata de Moisés.
O jardim do Paço Episcopal de Castelo Branco combina espaços ajardinados com lagos, fontes, canteiros e um conjunto de esculturas que representam temas religiosos e os reis de Portugal.
history:
O Jardim do Paço Episcopal de Castelo Branco foi construído no primeiro quartel do século XVIII, sob o patrocínio do Bispo D. João de Mendonça (1711–1736), junto ao edifício do Paço, que funcionava como residência de Inverno do Bispo da Guarda, que assim se protegia do frio excessivo daquela cidade. Em 1771, foi criada a Diocese de Castelo Branco e o Palácio transformou-se em residência oficial do Bispo. Todavia, o jardim só viria a ser terminado em finais do século XVIII, por D. Vicente Ferrer da Rocha, segundo Bispo de Castelo Branco, coadjuvado por Frei Daniel Joaquim do Rosário.  
No início do século XX, o jardim foi adquirido pela Câmara Municipal de Castelo Branco, tendo sido construído um novo patamar de acesso ao terraço central. A decoração deste novo espaço é constituída por canteiros talhados em buxo e por painéis de azulejos que representam os vários bispos do bispado de Castelo Branco.
keywords: Jardim, alegoria, virtudes teologais e cardinais, fontes; Castelo Branco.
tags: Jardim, alegoria, virtudes teologais e cardinais, fontes

ar.name: صحن مزين بزخرفة نجمية.
description:
ينتمي هذا الصحن المقعر بدون شفة، الملون بالأزرق فوق طلاء زجاجي حاو للقصدير الأبيض، إلى الأواني المنزلية المسماة "طبسيل"، والتي كانت تستخدم كأطباق لتقديم الصلصات. ترتكز تركيبته الهندسية الكلاسيكية حول مركز، تجسده دائرة زرقاء، محاطة بضفائر زهرية وبنقاط صغيرة تربطها مع نجمة سداسية الرؤوس. تنبعث من هذه النجمة المحاطة بشريط أزرق وبشُريْطة بيضاء، ثلاثة صفوف من دوائر متقاطعة على شكل زهرة ذات ستة بتلات. وزينت الفضاءات الداخلية لهذه التقاطعات، والمطلية بشكل متناوب باللون الأزرق الغامق والأزرق الباهت، بزخارف صغيرة أفعوانية بسيطة وبزخارف متكررة مزهرة، مستلهمة من تزهرات الصحون الصينية الزرقاء والبيضاء. وبالفعل، فقد كانت هذه الأواني الخزفية الصينية معروفة إبان هذه الفترة في المغرب بفضل التبادلات التجارية مع الشرق الأقصى.  
تنتهي الزخرفة على حواف الصحن المقوسة في اتجاه الداخل، بباقات صغيرة من الورود والأوراق الملونة بالأزرق الغامق. وقد كتب فوق الرصيعات الستة، المتوضعة على نهايات النجمة المركزية، حرفان عربيان بشكل مبسط وأربعة أرقام، تشير إلى عام صناعة هذه القطعة (1274 هجري/ 1857-1858 ميلادي). إن هذا التركيب المتطور للغاية والذي تنظم إيقاعاته تدرجات مختلفة من اللون الأزرق بارزة فوق اللمعان الأبيض للطلاء الزجاجي الحاوي للقصدير، قد أعطى أهمية لهذا الصحن الذي يشكل واحداً من خمسة قطع معروفة ضمن مجموعة أواني الفخار التي تحمل تأريخاً.

يعتبرُ هذا الصحن المقعر من نوع الأواني المنزلية المسماة ب"طبسيل" والمستعملة لتقديم الأطباق المحتوية على الصلصات، واحدا من بين خمس قطع تحملُ تاريخا. تنتظم تركيبته الكلاسيكية المتقنة الصنع حول مركز؛ وتذكر زخارفه النباتية الصغيرة بتزاويق بعض الصحون الصينية الزرقاء.
keywords: أثاث؛ زخرفة نباتية؛ زخرفة زهرية؛ زخرفة هندسية؛ فخار مطلي؛ تأثيرات صينية؛ طبسيل؛ أواني منزلية؛ تأثيرات صينية؛ صحن.
materials: فخار مطلي بالمينا الحاوية للقصدير؛ وطلاء من أكسيد الكوبالت والنيكل.

en.name: Star dish.
description:
This deep dish, painted with blue on a stanniferous (tin-bearing) white base, has no inner brim and belongs to the group of utensils known as *tabsil*, which were used to serve dishes in sauce. Its classical geometric composition is based around a centrepiece consisting of a blue circle surrounded by festoons and small dots that link to a six-pointed star. Three lines of intertwined circles radiate from this star, which is highlighted with a blue braid and a white ribbon, before opening out into a six-petal corolla. The spaces in the intertwining pattern, alternating between strong and faded blues, contains small snake motifs left in reserve and half-flower motifs inspired by the efflorescence of blue-and-white Chinese dishes, which were known at this time in Morocco as a result of trade with the Far East.  
The decoration is completed on the curved brim of the dish with small bouquets of flowers and foliage coloured deep blue. The six medallions placed on the points of the central star are inscribed in reserve with two Arabic letters and four numbers indicating the year when the object was made (AH 1274 / AD 1857–8). This very elaborate composition, based on different shades of blue on the brilliant white background, makes this dish particularly interesting. It is one of five known pieces of this type of ceramic to be dated.

This bowl, from a group of utensils known as *tabsil* used to serve dishes with sauce, is one of five pieces to be dated. Its highly elaborate, classical composition radiates from the centre. The small, blue seedlings are reminiscent of certain motifs on blue Chinese dishes.
keywords: vegetal decoration; floral decoration; geometric decoration
materials: Tin-glazed earthenware painted with nickel and cobalt oxide.
tags: Tin-glazed earthenware painted with nickel and cobalt oxide.

es.name: Fuente con estrella.
description:
PFuente cóncava sin borde, pintada de azul sobre una capa estannífera blanca. Pertenece a los utensilios denominados *tabsil*, que se empleaban para servir los platos en su salsa.  
La tradicional composición geométrica se desarrolla alrededor de un centro compuesto por un círculo azul ribeteado con festones y con puntitos que conectan con una estrella de seis puntas.  
Tres series de círculos entrecruzados que componen una corola de seis pétalos irradian de esta estrella, realzada con un galón azul y una cinta blanca. El interior de las intersecciones, donde alternan el color azul intenso y el azul descolorido, está decorado con pequeños diseños serpentiformes aislados y semiflorales inspirados en las florescencias de los platos chinos en azul y blanco. En efecto, en esta época ya se conocía en Marruecos ese tipo de porcelana gracias a los intercambios comerciales con el Extremo Oriente.  
La decoración se prolonga hasta los rebordes curvados de la fuente a modo de ramilletes de flores y follaje de color azul intenso. Sobre los seis medallones ubicados en las puntas de la estrella se distinguen dos letras árabes y cuatro cifras, todas ellas aisladas, que indican el año de fabricación del objeto (1274/1857-1858).  
Esta fuente se distingue por su elaborada composición en armonía con las diferentes tonalidades de azul, que destacan sobre el brillo blanco del vidriado estannífero; además, es una de las cinco piezas fechadas de esta serie de cerámicas.

Esta fuente, de la serie de utensilios denominados *tabsil*, que se empleaban para servir los platos en su salsa, es una de las cinco piezas que incluyen la fecha. Su composición clásica muy elaborada se articula alrededor de un centro. Los pequeños semilleros vegetales recuerdan algunas decoraciones de platos chinos azules.
materials: Cerámica con vidriado estannífero, pintura al óxido de cobalto y níquel.
tags: Cerámica con vidriado estannífero, pintura al óxido de cobalto y níquel.

fr.name: Plat étoilé.
description:
Ce plat creux sans marli, peint en bleu sur couverte stannifère blanche, appartient aux ustensiles dénommés *tabsil*, qui étaient utilisés pour servir les plats en sauce. Sa classique composition géométrique s'articule autour d'un centre matérialisé par un cercle bleu entouré de festons et de petits points qui établissent le lien avec une étoile à six branches. De cette étoile, soulignée d'un galon bleu et d'un ruban blanc, rayonnent trois rangées de cercles qui s'entrecroisent, pour s'épanouir en une corolle à six pétales. L'intérieur des entrecroisements, alternativement peints en un bleu soutenu et un bleu délavé, sont meublés de petits motifs serpentiformes laissés en réserve et de semis floraux inspirés des efflorescences des plats chinois bleu et blanc. Ces potiches étaient en effet connues à cette époque au Maroc, grâce aux échanges commerciaux avec l'Extrême-Orient.  
  
Le décor se termine sur les bords incurvés du plat par des petits bouquets de fleurs et de feuillage colorés d'un bleu soutenu. Sur les six médaillons posés sur les pointes de l'étoile centrale sont inscrits en réserve deux lettres arabes et quatre chiffres qui indiquent l'année de fabrication de cet objet (1274 H / 1857-1858 J.-C.). Cette composition très élaborée, rythmée par les différents dégradés de bleu qui se détachent sur l'éclat blanc de la couverte stannifère, fait l'intérêt de ce plat, qui est par ailleurs l'une des cinq pièces connues de cette série de céramiques à porter une datation.

Ce plat creux, de la série des ustensiles dénommés *tabsil*, utilisés pour servir les plats en sauce, est l'une des cinq pièces qui portent une datation. Sa composition classique très élaborée s'articule autour d'un centre. Les petits semis végétaux rappellent certains décors de plats chinois bleus.
keywords: mobilier ; décoration végétale ; décoration florale ; décoration géométrique
materials: Faïence émaillée à glaçure stannifère et peinture à l’oxyde de cobalt et nickel.
tags: Faïence émaillée à glaçure stannifère et peinture à l’oxyde de cobalt et nickel.

en.name: Report on the behaviour of Rustam Pasha
short_description: A report on Rustem Pasha, the *mutasarrif* or governor of Mount Lebanon, and his treatment of his subjects. The report describes him as a tyrannical and unjust governor with oppressive policies, curbing the autonomy of tribunals, for example. He also imposed high taxes on the tobacco trade in Mount Lebanon and ignored many of the Sultan's decrees.
keywords: Manuscript; Handwritten

en.name: Chapel of Our Lady of the Doctrine
description: The main image of this chapel represents Our Lady of the Doctrine (St. Ann with the Virgin Mary in her arms). Although the chapel was built in the 17th century, the decoration is typical of the Portuguese Baroque “National style”, which developed during the late 17th and early 18th century. This side chapel is the only one where gilded woodwork covers the whole of the interior surface including the barrel-vaulted ceiling.
dates: Work on the chapel began on 1 April 1634 and it was used by the Brotherhood of Our Lady of the Doctrine as their headquarters. The stonework was finally completed in 1690.
place: Church Interior, Church of São Roque
artist: The woodwork is by José Rodrigues Ramalho (1660–1721) according to a contract dated 1688 between him and the Brotherhood. The stonework was executed by master masons, Manuel Antunes and João Teixeira, whose exact dates are unknown.
partner: Institute for the Administration of Architectural and Archaeological Heritage -  IGESPAR

pt.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora da Doutrina
description: A imagem principal desta capela representa Nossa Senhora da Doutrina (Santa Ana com a Virgem Maria nos braços). Embora a capela tenha sido construída no século XVII, a sua decoração data de uma época mais tardia, típica do Barroco português, conhecido por “Estilo Nacional”, que se desenvolveu nos finais do século XVII e início do século XVIII. Esta é única capela lateral cuja talha dourada reveste toda a sua superfície interior, incluindo o tecto em abóbada.
dates: A capela foi iniciada em 1 de Abril de 1634, pela Irmandade de Nossa Senhora da Doutrina, que a usou como sua sede de culto; o trabalho de pedraria ficou completo em 1690.
artist: O trabalho é atribuído a José Rodrigues Ramalho, de acordo com um contrato escrito entre este mestre entalhador e a Irmandade. O trabalho de pedraria foi executado pelos mestres pedreiros Manuel Antunes e João Teixeira.

en.name: Bridal breast jewellery (*Chaprag*)
names: Chaprag – Nevestinski ukras za na gadi
short_description: This exquisite article called a *chaprag* shows the exceptional skill and inventiveness of the unknown goldsmith, who makes each piece of jewellery a virtual work of art in itself. The *chaprag* is a breast ornament consisting of a round plate and tiny chains. It is executed in filigree technique and adorned with decorative stones. Besides its decorative function, it was applied for the purpose of fastening the cleavage of the tunic. It was characteristic of the Ohrid-Prespa region, that is, the areas of Ohridsko Pole, Strushko Pole and Debarski Drimkol.
keywords: Breast ornament; coin; coinage; currency; numismatics; accessories; costume; wedding; marriage

en.name: Great ‘Umari Mosque
description:
The Great ‘Umari Mosque measuring 66.5 m. × 65.5 m., is a composite of several architectural styles that developed during various successive periods; the most important of which was the Mamluk period. The mosque was largely ruined during the Second World War, although the Supreme Islamic Council renovated it in 1924.  
The oldest part of the mosque, which has a basilica plan, dates to the Crusader period. This was the Cathedral dedicated to St John the Baptist, which was built on the site of the Friday Mosque, and was in the city centre during the early Islamic period. It consists of a central nave flanked by two aisles, all covered with cross vaults. The main entrance portal is on its west wall, above which is a circular window. The design of the portal with its columns, capitals and arches are in the Gothic style. On either side of the nave is a row of pillars and composite Byzantine marble columns crowned with what seem to be re-used Corinthian capitals.  
After the Crusaders departed the city in 583/1187, the building was converted into a Friday Mosque, and thus regained its old name: the “‘Umari Mosque”. In the Mamluk period, Sultan al-Mansur Husam al-Din Lajin (696/1297–698/1299) added to the mosque the eastern portal, which leads directly into the central nave of the early building (the basilica), and a minaret. The latter collapsed as a result of an earthquake, but was rebuilt before the First World War. The *amir* Sunqur al-‘Ala’i, the Viceroy of Gaza in 697/1297–1298, supervised the renovation works. He added a window and a portal to the northern wall of the basilica.  
The Amir Tankiz al-Nasiri, the Viceroy of Syria, supervised the second main additions to the building in 730/1329–1330. The basilica’s southern wall was removed and an additional aisle, in the style of the Crusader period, was added. Another entrance portal to the mosque was built in the southern wall, which leads to al-Qaysariyya (the Gold Market) and which also once led to Khan al-Zayt, which no longer exists.  
To the north of the old building is a courtyard surrounded by porticoes from the east, west and south. The southern portico, which was built in the 11th/17th century, faces the courtyard through a triple-arched colonnade, and is covered by three cross vaults with shallow domes. The eastern and western corridors were built at the end of the 12th/18th century. In the southern portico, there is a Mamluk-period *minbar* and a *mihrab*, both of which were moved from the Mosque of Sultan Qaytbay. The western entrance portal, and a number of the porticoes that lie behind it, were constructed at the end of the 13th/19th century.

es.name: Mezquita Mayor al-‘Umari
description:
La Mezquita Mayor al-‘Umari (66,5 × 65,5 m) es un edificio heteróclito, resultado de sucesivas etapas arquitectónicas, entre las que destaca la época mameluca. Durante la Primera Guerra Mundial buena parte de la mezquita fue destruida, pero el Consejo Islámico Supremo llevó a cabo su reconstrucción en 1924.  
La fecha de construcción de la parte más antigua del edificio, que presenta una planta basilical, se remonta a la época de los cruzados. Era la catedral, puesta bajo la advocación de san Juan Bautista, que los cruzados habían levantado en el emplazamiento de la mezquita *aljama* o de los viernes, en el centro de la ciudad, a comienzos de la era islámica. Consta de una nave central flanqueada por dos laterales, cubiertas por bóvedas por arista. En el centro del muro oeste se abre la puerta de acceso principal, rematada por una ventana circular. Esta entrada, con sus columnas, capiteles y arcos, es de estilo gótico. A ambos lados de la nave se eleva una hilera de pilares y columnas bizantinas de mármol, coronadas por capiteles de estilo corintio reutilizados.  
Tras la partida de los cruzados en 583/1187, el edificio fue transformado en Mezquita Mayor y recuperó su antigua denominación de “mezquita al-‘Umari”. En la época mameluca, el sultán al-Mansur Husam al-Din Layin (696/1297-698/1299) añadió la puerta este, que conduce directamente a la nave central del edificio primitivo (la basílica), e hizo erigir el alminar. Este se derrumbó a consecuencia de un terremoto, pero poco antes de la Primera Guerra Mundial fue reconstruido. El *emir* Sunqur al-‘Ala’i, vice-sultán de Gaza en 697/1297-1298, supervisó los trabajos de restauración y ordenó abrir una ventana y una puerta en el muro norte de la basílica.  
El *emir* Tankiz al-Nasiri, vice-sultán de Siria en 730/1329-1330, supervisó la segunda ampliación más importante. Hizo eliminar el muro sur del edificio de la basílica y construir una nave suplementaria. Se abrió en este muro sur otra entrada, que conducía a al-Qaysariyya (el zoco del Oro) y a Jan al-Zayt (del Aceite).  
Al norte del antiguo edificio hay un patio rodeado de pórticos en sus lados este, oeste y sur. El situado al sur fue construido en el siglo XI/XVII y da al patio a través de una columnata de tres arcos. Está cubierto por tres bóvedas por arista rebajadas. Las galerías este y oeste se remontan al siglo XII/XVIII. En el pórtico sur hay un *mimbar* y un *mihrab* de estilo mameluco, procedentes de la mezquita del sultán Qaytbay. A finales del siglo XIII/XIX se construyó la entrada oeste y algunos pórticos.

fr.name: Grande Mosquée de ‘Omar
description:
La Grande Mosquée de ‘Omar (66,5 m sur 65,5 m) est un bâtiment hétéroclite, le résultat de différentes évolutions architecturales successives. L’empreinte des Mamelouks y est prédominante. L’édifice a été largement détruit pendant la Première Guerre mondiale, mais le Conseil islamique suprême l’a fait restaurer en 1924.  
La partie la plus ancienne de la mosquée, qui présente un plan basilical, remonte à l’époque des Croisés. C’était la cathédrale, placée sous le vocable de Saint-Jean-Baptiste, que les Francs avaient érigée à l’emplacement de la Mosquée du Vendredi qui s’élevait au centre de la ville au début de l’ère islamique. Elle consiste en une nef centrale flanquée de deux bas-côtés, tous couverts de voûtes d’arêtes. La porte d’entrée principale s’ouvre dans le mur occidental, surmonté d’un oculus. Le portail principal, avec ses colonnes, ses chapiteaux et ses arcs, est de style gothique. De chaque côté de la nef s’élève une rangée de piliers et de colonnes byzantines composites en marbre couronnées de chapiteaux de remploi, vraisemblablement corinthiens.  
Après le départ des Croisés en 583/1187, le bâtiment fut transformé en Grande Mosquée et récupéra ainsi son ancienne dénomination de “mosquée de ‘Omar”. À l’époque mamelouke, le sultan al-Mansour Hussam al-Din Lajin (696/1297- 698/1299) ajouta le portail oriental, qui conduit directement à la nef centrale de l’édifice primitif (la basilique), et fit ériger le minaret. Ce dernier s’effondra à la suite d’un séisme, mais il a été reconstruit juste avant la Première Guerre mondiale. C’est l’émir Sunqur al-‘Ala’i, vice-sultan de Gaza en 697/1297-1298, qui supervisa les travaux de restauration. Il ajouta une fenêtre et un portail au mur nord de la basilique.  
C’est à l’émir Tankiz al-Nasiri, le vicesultan de Syrie en 730/1329-1330, que sont dues les secondes adjonctions majeures. Il fit abattre le mur méridional de la basilique et élever une nef supplémentaire. Le mur méridional fut percé d’une autre entrée, qui conduit à al-Qaysariyya (le marché de l’Or) et à Khan al-Zayt.  
Au nord de l’ancien bâtiment se trouve une cour entourée de portiques sur les côtés est, ouest et sud. Le portique méridional, qui date du XIe/XVIIe siècle, donne sur la cour par une colonnade de trois arcs. Il est couvert par trois voûtes d’arêtes surbaissées. Les galeries orientale et occidentale ont été construites à la fin du XIIe/XVIIIe siècle. Dans le portique sud se trouvent un *minbar* et un *mihrab* d’époque mamelouke; tous deux proviennent de la mosquée du sultan Qaytbay. Le portail d’entrée occidental a été ajouté à la fin du XIIIe/XIXe siècle, ainsi qu’un certain nombre de portiques.

en.name: *St. Roch* and *St. Sebastian*
description:
These splendidly colourful Rococo statues of *St. Roch* and *St. Sebastian* came to the museum from the parish church of Egervár in the county of Zala. The patron of the church, Count Ignác Széchényi, commissioned a new large tabernacle with six carved figures for the high altar of the church, made in around 1730, in 1757. The Széchényi family already had connections with artists in Graz, the area where Philipp Jakob Straub chose to settle and work.  
Both statues are of saints believed to be protectors from the plague, and both express pain and suffering. *St. Roch*, dressed in pilgrim's clothes, turns his eyes heavenward. His lips parted in pain, he points to the wound on his foot. Next to him is the dog that allegedly brought him bread when he was suffering from the plague. Bound to a tree and wounded by arrows, the young martyr, *St. Sebastian*, is resigned to his fate. His head rests on his shoulder and tears drip from his closed eyes. *St. Roch*'s garments flutter in deep folds, providing the contrast of light and shade, while light glides softly on the sensuously beautiful body of *St. Sebastian*.  
The statues are promoted into the vanguard of Rococo sculpture in Hungary by the outstanding quality of modelling, the subtle and reserved colouring and the empathic rendering of emotions.  
Philipp Jakob Straub was born into the Württenberg family of sculptors and moved to Vienna with his brother, Johann Baptist Straub (later court sculptor in Munich), in 1727. Philipp Jakob Straub studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna from 1730 to 1733, at which time he settled in Graz. In Graz he worked on commissions for the church, the aristocracy and the middle class, both in wood and in stone. On stylistic grounds, research attributes to him an extensive oeuvre in Styria where he introduced the influence of Bavarian Rococo sculpture and the practices of stone sculpture from the court in Vienna.

The high altar in the parish church of Egervár (c. 1730) contained tabernacle statues – two of which were *St. Roch* and *St. Sebastian* – and all of which were commissioned from Styria in 1757. Documents relating to count Széchenyi's relationship with the church and the artist helped to confirm the attribution of these works to Philipp Jakob Straub, a member of the South-German Straub family. Straub settled in Graz and brought fine Rococo sculpture to the Transdanubian region.

en.name: Portrait of Wadih Sabra
short_description: Wadih Sabra was the composer of the Ottoman anthem, used today as the Lebanese National anthem. He also established the Institute of Music in Beirut, as decreed by Sultan 'Abd al-Hamid in 1910, and founded the National Conservatory. He was the founder of the first musical-scientific journal of its kind in the Arab region, and wrote the first Arabic language opera.

en.name: Gold to the country from the [Italian] colony in Tunisia
names: Receipt for the donation of gold to Italy, in support of its war effort during World War I
short_description:
This receipt certified that Leone Moreno (Tunis, 1852-1940) “donated gold to the country” in order to support Italy’s war effort during WWI. Leone was the grandchild of Mosè Moreno, a Jew from Livorno who migrated to Tunis around 1830. In Tunisia, the Morenos became successful in business. Leone’s father and brothers were traders and bankers, while Leone was an agricultural entrepreneur.  
He was a nationalist and was one of the Italians who actively resisted the French policy of assimilating the Italians in Tunisia. He employed only Italian workers on his estate and supported the Società Dante Alighieri, a society aimed at promoting Italian language and culture abroad. Leone Moreno also generously supported the Italian hospital Giuseppe Garibaldi and the Italian orphanage “Principe di Piemonte”.

en.name: City Centre
description:
Castellamare del Golfo was an emporium of the city of Segesta; the place where the Elimians had directed their maritime traffic up to 827 when the Muslims occupied it. In perennial contrast with the Greeks of nearby Selinunte the important centre of the Elimians turned round the Carthaginian power, which made the emporium of Segesta one of the most important fortified stations of the northern basin of Sicily. The date of construction of the fortress is not known for certain, but it is recalled that the first nucleus could indeed go back to the Islamic period. It is exactly at this time that a tunny-fishery and the harbour were developed, serving also as a base for incursions to damage merchant traffic of Byzantium, and the construction of a loading-dock for the embarkation of grain. The Arabs baptised the centre *al-Madarij*, possibly on account of the presence of a craggy and very steep pathway. At the time of al-Idrisi the fortress  
of Castellamare was provided with “*a port in which there is a coming and going of ships and nets are kept there for fishing tunny*”. The present town is identified at a glance from its belvedere, along the main road.

es.name: Centro urbano
description: Castellammare del Golfo nació como emporio de la ciudad de Segesta, el lugar donde los elimos hacían su tráfico marítimo, hasta que en 827 fue ocupada por los musulmanes. En perpetua confrontación con los griegos de la vecina Selinunte, el importante centro elimo orbitó en torno a la potencia cartaginesa, que hizo del emporio segestano una de las más importantes estaciones fortificadas de la cuenca septentrional de Sicilia. No se sabe con certeza la fecha de construcción de la fortificación, pero se sostiene que el primer núcleo puede remontarse precisamente al periodo islámico. Justamente en este periodo se construyeron la atunara, el puerto, el cual sirvió también como base para las incursiones contra el tráfico mercantil de Bizancio, y un muelle de carga para el embarque del trigo. Los árabes bautizaron la villa como al-Madarish, es decir “las escaleras”, quizá por la existencia de una calle empinadísima. En tiempos de al-Idrisi, la fortaleza de Castellammare estaba provista de “un puerto que es un ir y venir de naves y a ellas sujetan redes para pescar los atunes”. La villa actual se descubre de un solo vistazo desde el mirador, situado en la carretera estatal.

en.name: Candlestick Base
description:
This large candlestick base decorated with six sitting high-relief lions is a truly unmatched piece of Iranian or Eastern Anatolian toreutics. The body of the object is made of a single metal sheet, a high-relief decor created by the technique of two-sided hammering. Finest treatment of animal faces, patterns of mane, fur and spiral vegetable sprouts between figures indicate elite status. On the shoulders between the animal heads there is an Arabic inscription with traditional blessings: "Glory, success, domination, happiness to the owner of this".  
The base was designed to stand on the floor and hold one large candle. The lion is an ancient Iranian symbol of royal majesty and charisma, king's power and triumph, in astrological context directly related to the sun.
keywords: Candlestick base; Metalwork; Copper alloy; Iran; Eastern Anatolia
partner: The Bohdan and Varvara Khanenko National Museum of Arts

en.name: Mosque lamp
description: This hammered brass lamp is decorated with openwork pattern inlaid with silver and a black compound. It was commissioned for the mausoleum of Mamluk ruler al-Malik al-Zahir Baybars (AH 620-675 / AD 1223–1277), constructed in Damascus in AH 675 AH / AD 1277. The inscription carries the words that plead God to sanctify the sultan's spirit and illumine his tomb. A tray would have accompanied this lamp, which when filled with oil and suspended, would have projected the inscriptions across the mausoleum.

en.name: Oil Exploration
description: Abdullah Al Muharraqi’s Oil Exploration can be used to discuss Bahrain’s pioneering role in the oil history of the Gulf and the beginning of a wider regional transformation. Oil was discovered in Bahrain in 1932, making it the first country in the Arabian Gulf to enter the oil era. This discovery preceded similar turning points in neighbouring states, including Kuwait and Saudi Arabia in 1938, Qatar in 1939–1940, Abu Dhabi in 1958, and Oman in 1964. By showing workers around an oil well, the painting presents oil exploration not only as a technical or economic event, but also as a human and social process. The work is therefore useful for explaining how Bahrain’s early oil discovery marked the beginning of a new regional history, shifting Gulf societies from older economies based on pearling, maritime trade, and local labour toward oil-based modernisation, infrastructure, migration, and state formation.
holder: Qatar Museums, Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art
keywords: oil exploration; Bahrain; Gulf; regional transformation

en.name: *Invasion of the French camp. The Swiss refuse to advance despite the interventions of their leaders*
description:
The famous series of seven Flemish tapestries depicting the Battle of Pavia entered the public collections as part of the 1862 bequest of Alfonso d’Avalos, who donated his family’s collection to the National Museum of Naples.  
Produced to be given to Emperor Charles V by the Estates-General of Brussels, on the occasion of the latter’s meeting in Brussels in 1531, the decorative series of tapestries was designed to celebrate the victory of the imperial troops over those of the French, under the command of Francis I. This victory, which occurred on 24 February 1525, was fought in the environs of the Visconti Park, at the gates of Pavia.  
Woven in Brussels, the tapestries were produced using designs by Bernard van Orley (now in the Louvre in Paris) in the workshop of William Dermoyen (or Van der Moyen), identified thanks to the presence of a weaver’s mark on the border of two tapestries in the series. Furthermore, the presence of the mark has allowed the years in which the series was produced to be established: that is, after 1528, the year in which a decree required tapestry workers to “sign” their products, and by the start of 1531, given that the tapestries would be presented to the Emperor in the March of that year.  
Recently, an interpretation of the entire cycle has been proposed that aims to recreate sequentially the landscape depicted in the seven tapestries as a single, panoramic, overview (Paredes 2014).  
This tapestry depicts one of the decisive moments of the Battle of Pavia: the civilians are escaping from the French encampment, which is being attacked by the imperial troops, in the vicinity of the Vernavola river, through the breaches made in the wall of Visconti Park during the siege. The episode provides an opportunity to show everyday narratives: a soldier in the foreground runs away, carrying off with him a couple of chickens, while he looks towards the viewer, involving us in the scene; a woman in the distance carries a basket with two geese; a friar, frightened, is running. In the foreground, the Swiss infantry (recognisable by the flag with a white cross) who had fought with the French, proving their courage and valour, all hope of victory lost and surrounded on all sides, yield to the imperial cavalry, throwing their pikes to the ground, deaf to the cries of their officers, and try to seek safety in flight or surrender. In the foreground, amongst the soldiers one can make out a drummer, a piper and a standard bearer with a longsword, figures who often recur in military iconography. The figure in the centre of the tapestry has been identified as the Swiss captain Jean de Diesbach, who offers himself up to the sword of the enemy cavalier so he can die with honour (Casali 1993).
artist: William Dermoyen atelier on a cartoon designed by Bernard van Orley

it.name: Invasione del campo francese. Gli svizzeri si rifiutano di avanzare nonostante gli interventi dei loro capi
description:
La celebre serie dei sette arazzi fiamminghi della Battaglia di Pavia, esposti in una grande sala del museo di Capodimonte, entra nelle raccolte pubbliche con il legato testamentario del 1862 di Alfonso d’Avalos che dona al Museo Nazionale di Napoli la collezione di famiglia.  
Realizzata per essere donata dagli stati Generali di Bruxelles all’imperatore Carlo V, in occasione della riunione degli stessi a Bruxelles nel 1531, la serie decorativa intendeva celebrare la vittoria delle truppe imperiali su quelle francesi, comandate da Francesco I, avvenuta il 24 febbraio del 1525, e combattuta nella zona del Parco Visconteo, alle porte di Pavia.  
Tessuti a Bruxelles, gli arazzi sono stati realizzati su disegni di Bernart van Orley (oggi a Parigi, Musée du Louvre), nell'atelier di Willem Dermoyen (o Van der Moyen), identificato grazie alla presenza del marchio del tessitore sulla bordure di due arazzi della serie. Inoltre, proprio la presenza del marchio ha permesso di stabilire gli anni di realizzazione del ciclo: cioè dopo il 1528, anno in cui un editto imponeva agli arazzieri di firmare i loro prodotti, e l'inizio del 1531, dato che verrà donato nel mese di marzo all'imperatore.  
Recentemente è stata proposta una lettura d’insieme del ciclo, tesa a ricostruire in sequenza il paesaggio rappresentato nei sette arazzi in un’unica, e panoramica, visione d’insieme (Paredes 2014).  
Nel panno vi è raffigurato uno dei momenti conclusivi della battaglia di Pavia: i civili fuggono dal campo francese attaccato dagli imperiali, nei pressi della Vernavola, attraverso le brecce praticate nel muro del Parco Visconteo durante l’assedio. L'episodio offre lo spunto per narrazioni di carattere quotidiano: un soldato in primo piano fugge portando via alcuni polli, mentre guarda verso lo spettatore coinvolgendolo nella scena, una donna sullo sfondo porta un cesto con due oche, un frate corre impaurito. In primo piano, i fanti svizzeri (riconoscibli per la bandiera con la croce bianca) che avevano combattuto al seguito dei francesi dando prova di coraggio e di valore, perduta ogni speranza di vittoria e circondati da ogni parte, si arrendono ai cavalieri imperiali, gettando a terra le picche, sordi ai richiami dei loro ufficiali, e cercano scampo con la fuga o con la resa. In primo piano, tra i soldati si distinguono un suonatore di tamburo, di piffero e un alfiere portaspadone, figure che ricorrono spesso nell'iconografia militare. Il personaggio al centro dell'arazzo, è stato identificato con il capitano svizzero Jean de Diesbac, che si offre alla spada del cavaliere nemico per morire con onore (Casali 1993).

artist: Atelier di William Dermoyen su disegni di Bernard van Orley
materials: Lana, seta, cotone colorato con fili d'oro e d'argento

en.name: Small-Pattern "Holbein" Carpet with Closed Kufesque Border
description: A so-called "Holbein" rug with a heavily stylized pseudo-*kufic* inscription around the border. The red field has a pattern of nine rows of small medallions alternately white and blue. Knotted bands in pink, red, and violet define the white medallions which enclose various rosettes in octagons in the above colors. The blue medallions are formed by arabesques in blue and green with cross motifs, in the above colors, within lozenges. The rug is bordered by interlaced angular bands, derived from *kufic* writing, in white, red, blue, and green on a violet or red ground. The inner and outer guard bands contain a ribbon design in red, blue, green, and violet on a yellow, and partly on a red ground.
